title: Category Theory
body:
The mathematics [[Monad]] comes from, and the course went far enough into it to derive the
definition rather than assert it. The subject's move is to study objects **only** through the
arrows between them: never ask what a thing is made of, only what maps into and out of it.

## A category

A category $\mathcal{C}$ is:

- a collection of **objects** $A, B, C, \dots$
- for each pair, a collection of **morphisms** (arrows) $f : A \to B$
- a **composition** operation: given $f : A \to B$ and $g : B \to C$, an arrow
  $g \circ f : A \to C$
- an **identity** arrow $\mathrm{id}_A : A \to A$ for every object

subject to two laws:

$$\mathrm{id}_B \circ f = f = f \circ \mathrm{id}_A \qquad\qquad h \circ (g \circ f) = (h \circ g) \circ f$$

Identity and associativity, which is the same shape as the [[Monad]] laws and as a monoid in
[[Abstract Algebra]] (a [[Group]] without inverses). That recurrence is not a coincidence and it
is most of why the subject is useful: it names a pattern that keeps appearing.

Note what is *not* required. Objects have no elements. An arrow is not necessarily a function.
The only thing you may do with arrows is compose them, and everything in the theory is built
from that restriction.

| Category | Objects | Arrows |
|---|---|---|
| **Set** | [[Sets\|sets]] | functions |
| **Hask** | Haskell types | Haskell functions |
| a preorder | elements | one arrow $a \to b$ iff $a \le b$ |
| a monoid | one single object | its elements, composing by the operation |

**Hask** is the one this course lives in: objects are types like `Int` and `[String]`, arrows
are functions, composition is `.`, and identity is `id`. The category laws are then facts about
Haskell you already believed, which is the point of setting it up.

## Functors

A **functor** $F : \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}$ maps objects to objects and arrows to arrows,
preserving the structure:

$$F(\mathrm{id}_A) = \mathrm{id}_{F(A)} \qquad\qquad F(g \circ f) = F(g) \circ F(f)$$

In **Hask** the object map is the type constructor (`Maybe` takes `Int` to `Maybe Int`) and the
arrow map is `fmap`. Written out, the two laws are `fmap id = id` and
`fmap (g . h) = fmap g . fmap h`, which is exactly what [[Functor]] states. **Haskell's Functor
class is the categorical definition with no changes**, restricted to functors from Hask to
itself. Such a functor is an **endofunctor**, and that word is now one third of the famous
sentence.

## Natural transformations

A map between *functors*. Given $F, G : \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}$, a natural transformation
$\eta : F \Rightarrow G$ gives, for every object $A$, an arrow $\eta_A : F(A) \to G(A)$, such
that for every $f : A \to B$ the square commutes:

$$G(f) \circ \eta_A = \eta_B \circ F(f)$$

In Haskell that reads: a polymorphic function `eta :: forall a. F a -> G a`, and the condition
is `fmap f . eta = eta . fmap f`. **Repackage the container, then map, or map, then repackage,
and you get the same answer.**

```haskell
safeHead :: [a] -> Maybe a           -- a natural transformation from [] to Maybe
listToMaybe, maybeToList, reverse, concat   -- all natural transformations
```

The reason it is called *natural* is the good part: the condition is automatic. A function of
type `forall a. F a -> G a` cannot inspect its elements ([[Parametric Polymorphism]]), so it
can only rearrange structure, and rearranging commutes with mapping. **Naturality is
parametricity**, and the free theorem for that signature *is* the commuting square. So in
Haskell you never check naturality; the type gives it to you.

## The sentence, unpacked

> A monad is a monoid in the category of endofunctors.

A monad on $\mathcal{C}$ is an endofunctor $T$ with two natural transformations:

$$\eta : \mathrm{Id} \Rightarrow T \qquad\qquad \mu : T \circ T \Rightarrow T$$

satisfying $\mu \circ T\mu = \mu \circ \mu T$ (associativity) and
$\mu \circ T\eta = \mathrm{id} = \mu \circ \eta T$ (identity). Endofunctors compose, and
composition gives the category of endofunctors a multiplication; $\mu$ is that multiplication
and $\eta$ is its unit, so the axioms are the monoid axioms. That is the whole sentence.

Translated:

| Category theory | Haskell |
|---|---|
| endofunctor $T$ | a [[Functor]] instance, `m` |
| $\eta : \mathrm{Id} \Rightarrow T$ | `return :: a -> m a` |
| $\mu : T^2 \Rightarrow T$ | `join :: m (m a) -> m a` |
| associativity, identity | the three [[Monad]] laws |

Haskell's `>>=` is `join` and `fmap` packaged together, and the two definitions are
interderivable:

```haskell
m >>= f  =  join (fmap f m)
join mm  =  mm >>= id
```

`fmap f m` produces the nested `m (m b)` that the staircase in [[Monad]] complains about, and
`join` is the flattening. So bind is not a primitive idea at all, it is "map, then flatten",
and `concatMap` for lists is literally `concat . map`.

## Is it needed

No. You can use [[Monad]] competently having never seen a commuting square, and most working
Haskell programmers do. What the theory buys is an explanation of why the laws are those laws
rather than a list to memorise, and why the same three-rung ladder shows up in unrelated types.
It answers "why", not "how".

## Core Facts to Know

- A category is objects, arrows, composition, and identities, with identity and associativity laws.
- Objects have no interior; everything is said with arrows.
- **Hask**: objects are Haskell types, arrows are functions, composition is `.`.
- A **functor** maps objects and arrows and preserves identity and composition.
- Haskell's [[Functor]] class is that definition for endofunctors on Hask; `fmap` is the arrow map.
- An **endofunctor** maps a category to itself.
- A **natural transformation** maps one functor to another, commuting with `fmap`.
- In Haskell it is a `forall a. F a -> G a`, and naturality is free by [[Parametric Polymorphism]].
- A monad is an endofunctor plus $\eta$ (`return`) and $\mu$ (`join`) obeying monoid axioms.
- Endofunctors compose, so they form a monoid-like structure: hence "monoid in the category of endofunctors".
- `m >>= f = join (fmap f m)` and `join mm = mm >>= id`; bind is map-then-flatten.
- `concatMap = concat . map` is that identity for lists.
